title: #BIS-easiness of Boolean log-supermodular counting CSPs
formal:
For every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\) of functions \(f:\{0,1\}^{r_f}\to\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\), where each arity \(r_f\geq0\) is fixed, does
\[\bigl[\forall f\in\mathcal F\ \forall x,y\in\{0,1\}^{r_f},\quad f(x\lor y)f(x\land y)\geq f(x)f(y)\bigr]\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\#\operatorname{CSP}(\mathcal F)\leq_{\mathrm{AP}}\#\mathrm{BIS}\ ?\]
Here \(\leq_{\mathrm{AP}}\) is a randomized approximation-preserving reduction for counting problems with the relative-error and polynomial-cost guarantees below. The family is fixed before instances arrive, and a reduction may depend on it.
definitions:
For bit vectors \(x,y\), the vectors \(x\land y\) and \(x\lor y\) are their coordinatewise minimum and maximum. A function satisfying the displayed inequality is log-supermodular, abbreviated LSM. This multiplicative definition allows zero values and never requires taking the logarithm of zero. Each function table consists of fixed nonnegative rational values, and is not supplied as part of an instance. The family may be empty and its members may have arbitrarily large fixed finite arity.

An instance \(I\) of \(\#\operatorname{CSP}(\mathcal F)\) has variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), \(n\geq0\), and an explicitly listed sequence of \(m\geq0\) constraints \(f_j(x_{i_{j,1}},\ldots,x_{i_{j,r_j}})\), with \(f_j\in\mathcal F\). Repeated variables within a tuple, repeated constraints and unused variables are allowed. Constraint multiplicity matters and is represented by repetition in the list, not a binary-encoded multiplicity. The partition function is the nonnegative rational number
\[Z_{\mathcal F}(I)=\sum_{\sigma:[n]\to\{0,1\}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}f_j\bigl(\sigma(i_{j,1}),\ldots,\sigma(i_{j,r_j})\bigr).\]
An empty product is one, so a constraint-free instance has value \(2^n\). A nullary function contributes its constant value. No unary function, pinning constraint or arbitrary rational weight is freely added to the fixed family.

Encode \(n,m\) in unary, followed by the fixed-family index for each constraint and its variable indices in binary, with delimiters. Write \(L\) for this total bit length. The accuracy parameter is a rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) supplied as binary numerator and denominator; \(b\) is its encoding length. Algorithms operate on finite binary strings with ordinary bit costs. Malformed instances can be rejected. The finite fixed tables may be built into the program; no real-number oracle or varying-language uniformity is used.

The problem \(\#\mathrm{BIS}\) takes a finite simple bipartite graph \(G=(U,V,E)\), with its two disjoint vertex classes explicitly supplied, and counts all subsets \(S\subseteq U\cup V\) containing no adjacent pair. Vertices, including isolated ones, are explicitly listed; edges are listed by binary endpoint indices. There is no degree bound. The empty independent set is counted, so \(\#\mathrm{BIS}(G)\geq1\).

A randomized approximation scheme for a nonnegative counting function \(Z\) returns a nonnegative rational estimate \(\widehat Z\) such that, for every valid input and accuracy,
\[\Pr[(1-\varepsilon)Z\leq\widehat Z\leq(1+\varepsilon)Z]\geq3/4.\]
If \(Z=0\), the successful estimate is exactly zero. A fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS) additionally has running time polynomial in \(L+b+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil\), for every outcome of its fair independent random bits. The sources use \(e^{-\varepsilon}Z\leq\widehat Z\leq e^{\varepsilon}Z\); rescaling the requested tolerance gives the same approximation class and reduction notion. The card retains its original relative \((1\pm\varepsilon)\) convention.

An AP-reduction consists of a randomized oracle Turing machine \(M_{\mathcal F}\) and a polynomial \(p_{\mathcal F}\). On every \((I,\varepsilon)\), its own bit computation, number and encoded sizes of queries, and output length are bounded by \(p_{\mathcal F}(L+b+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)\), independently of random bits. A query requests an approximation to \(\#\mathrm{BIS}(G)\) at rational tolerance \(\delta\in(0,1)\), with \(1/\delta\) bounded by that polynomial. Whenever the oracle is a randomized approximation scheme for #BIS, independent invocations of it must make the resulting machine an approximation scheme for \(Z_{\mathcal F}\). The probability bound includes both the reduction’s randomness and oracle failures. Confidence can be amplified by polynomially many independent calls and a median; exact counting is not provided. The cost of the oracle’s internal computation is not charged as a unit-cost exact-counting computation: the defining consequence is that substituting any FPRAS for #BIS yields an FPRAS for the source problem. Reading, writing and processing the polynomial-length estimates and query encodings are charged to the reduction.

The quantifiers are \(\forall\mathcal F\ \exists M_{\mathcal F},p_{\mathcal F}\ \forall I,\varepsilon\), for LSM families. No single algorithm constructing reductions from arbitrary input function tables is required. No assumption that #BIS has an FPRAS, or that it lacks one, is part of the proposition.

context_blocks.text: Approximate counting asks for the total weight of all assignments, even when merely finding a satisfying assignment is easy. The question treats #BIS as a comparison problem: a positive answer transfers any efficient randomized approximation scheme for that benchmark to every fixed rational Boolean LSM family. It does not itself supply an approximation scheme for #BIS.

Implication is the zero-one binary function IMP(a,b) that vanishes only at (1,0). It is log-supermodular. Products of implication and unary factors, followed by sums over auxiliary Boolean variables, give important #BIS-easy constructions. Taking suitable limits broadens their expressive power, but still does not generate every log-supermodular function.

A concrete obstruction is the rational four-ary function
\[g(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=\begin{cases}4,&\sum_i x_i=4,\\2,&\sum_i x_i=3,\\1,&\sum_i x_i\leq2.\end{cases}\]
The source proves that \(g\) is log-supermodular but cannot be generated from implication and arbitrary nonnegative unary functions by finite products, summation over auxiliary variables, identification of coordinates, equality constraints and uniform limiting operations. This defeats a general expressibility argument of that form; it does not prove that \(\#\operatorname{CSP}(\{g\})\) lacks a more general AP-reduction. Such reductions may make randomized, adaptive approximation queries instead of representing each local function by one gadget.

The conservative counting-CSP classification allows every unary function and examines all finite sublanguages. In its intermediate region the proved upper bound is reduction to some Boolean LSM language. For arity at most two the stronger #BIS upper bound is known. The present question asks whether that distinction between an LSM upper bound and a #BIS upper bound can always be removed.

Quantifying over every finite family already includes any chosen finite collection of unary functions, since all unary Boolean functions satisfy log-supermodularity. Thus the finite-language target covers the usual conservative finite-sublanguage interpretation without granting input-dependent real weights. Some LSM families are easy to count exactly, so the proposition asks for a universal upper reduction rather than asserting #BIS-hardness for every family.

Both the gadget limitation and the conservative theorem are established results; neither settles the full AP-reducibility question. Exact-counting dichotomies also use a different computational task. These distinctions explain why a broad positive-correlation condition has not automatically produced the requested comparison with #BIS.

why: A positive answer would collapse the whole finite rational Boolean log-supermodular approximation region to the #BIS benchmark and sharpen the conservative counting-CSP classification. A negative answer would separate general log-supermodularity from that benchmark at the level of computational reductions, beyond the known separation in gadget expressibility.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish, for every permitted finite rational LSM family, an AP-reduction with the uniform-in-instance cost, oracle accuracy, relative error and success guarantees above, including zero partition functions. A negative answer must establish a permitted finite family for which no such AP-reduction exists. Proving only a reduction for a special arity or function class, a failure of a particular gadget construction, exact-counting hardness, or a lower bound under an additional unproved complexity assumption does not establish the full unconditional target.

progress.text: The expressibility work identifies the central LSM region and proves that implication with unary functions fails to generate it already at arity four; this is a representation obstruction, not an AP-separation.
The checked v3 preprint and its 2015 journal publication establish conservative classifications with LSM-easiness in the general intermediate case and #BIS-easiness in the arity-at-most-two case.
The survey explicitly distinguishes the four-ary expressibility obstruction from the possibility of a broader #BIS AP-reduction, and retains LSM-easiness in its general theorem.

status_note: The checked 2015 conservative classification and the 2017 survey leave a gap between general Boolean LSM-easiness and #BIS-easiness. The survey explicitly says the known four-ary failure of implication-based expressibility does not rule out an AP-reduction. Bounded primary-source searches on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution of the full finite rational-family proposition; this is not an exhaustive certification of current openness. Preprint revision dates and journal publication dates are distinguished in the references.

sentences: A Boolean log-supermodular counting CSP sums products of nonnegative rational local weights over all Boolean assignments.
The question asks whether every fixed finite family of these weights admits a randomized approximation-preserving reduction to counting independent sets in bipartite graphs.
The reduction must control relative error, all oracle failures and polynomial bit cost, and must also handle zero total weight.
Known classifications give #BIS upper bounds in important special cases, while a four-variable gadget obstruction does not rule out more general reductions.
A resolution would determine whether the whole log-supermodular approximation region has #BIS as a common computational upper benchmark.
